title: Polasek's rise through the ranks to Mountain West rookie North Dakota St. was launched by hard labor
description: The effort and energy Tim Polasek has poured into North Dakota State's football program on the climb to the FBS can be easily sourced back to his rural roots. fullText:
FARGO, N.D. (AP) — The effort and energy Tim Polasek has poured into North Dakota State's football program on the climb to the FBS can be easily sourced back to his rural roots.

As a small-college quarterback on summer and winter breaks, and later to supplement a meager income as he launched a career in coaching, Polasek worked grueling jobs as a logger in the woods of central Wisconsin and on the overnight shift at a steel mill near his tiny hometown of Iola.

Appreciation for the unglamourous work as a small-college assistant sure comes quick with that background.

"I learned a lot there: That could be you if you don't graduate college and pursue something," said Polasek, who is 28-3 with the Bison since becoming head coach in 2024. "Seeing those tough jobs and other people having to execute that every day really always makes it an honor and a privilege to be the leader of this program."

Having handily beaten Jacksonville State and Fordham in their first two games, the Bison will face one of their biggest tests as a first-year FBS team on Saturday night: Their Mountain West Conference opener at Air Force.

Though five of the strongest programs — Boise State, Colorado State, Fresno State, San Diego State and Utah State — departed this year to restore the Pac-12, the Mountain West restocked with UTEP and North Dakota State and Northern Illinois as football-only members to join holdovers Air Force, Hawaii, Nevada, New Mexico, San Jose State, UNLV and Wyoming.

There's enough relative proximity to the league's geographic footprint and like-minded public institutions for NDSU to see a long-term home that now offers the chance — albeit an annual long shot — to make the College Football Playoff. The Bison won 10 national championships over two decades in the FCS after collecting eight national titles at lower levels.

"We weren't going to go just to go," athletic director Matt Larsen said. "It really had to be the right fit."

Polasek was offensive coordinator and quarterbacks coach at Wyoming from 2021-23 under head coach Craig Bohl, his former boss at NDSU. Having spent four seasons as the offensive line coach at Iowa before that, Polasek took the job at Wyoming with an eye toward becoming a head coach himself.

"It was really critical for me to go to Iowa and Wyoming and not be one of the top two or three teams picked in the preseason every year and learn those hard lessons," said Polasek, who turned 47 last month. "There was always chatter that NDSU would fit in the Mountain West."

After becoming the all-time leading passer at Concordia University, an NCAA Division III school near Milwaukee, Polasek spent three years on staff at Wisconsin-Stevens Point. Then he got his first big break with a graduate assistant job under Bohl at North Dakota State, which was two seasons into a jump from Division II to the FCS.

He was put in charge of the running backs a year later, added tight ends to his responsibilities after three more seasons, and returned from a one-year stint at Northern Illinois in 2014 as NDSU's offensive coordinator and running backs coach under head coach Chris Klieman.

Then Polasek got a taste of Big Ten play at Iowa, learning the value of "being brilliant at the basics" under longtime head coach Kirk Ferentz before the jump to Wyoming.

"The second thing I learned from Coach Ferentz is if you treat people right you can cultivate an environment where it's fun to show up to work," Polasek said last month in his office at the Fargodome. "No matter if the portal or NIL and all this stuff exists or not, hey, let's treat each other with respect. Everybody in the building should be able to dance to the music the way they want to dance to it."

The upperclassmen on NDSU's roster were recruited by the previous staff under Matt Entz, who's now the head coach at Fresno State. Polasek's enthusiasm for and experience with the program was immediately palpable to those players.

"He's just hard-nosed and he loves football and he knows the game and he's a people person," said third-year wide receiver and kick returner Jackson Williams. "He's going to take care of us, but at the same time he's going to push us to our limits."

title: How to Watch: Michigan Football vs Oklahoma, other top games of Week 2
description: A Hail Mary was needed for the Michigan Wolverines to beat the Western Michigan Broncos on Saturday in one of the most surprising and controversial finishes in college football in Week 1. fullText:
A Hail Mary was needed for the Michigan Wolverines to beat the Western Michigan Broncos on Saturday in one of the most surprising and controversial finishes in college football in Week 1. But the question on the minds of just about every Michigan Wolverines fan this week is: "Was that just one bad game or a sign of things to come?"

Undisciplined and out-of-sync play on the offensive end sparks fears of a repeat of a 2025 season where Bryce Underwood and the offense never hit their stride enough for Michigan to compete. That will be put to the test against one of the best defenses in America on Saturday as the No. 11 Oklahoma Sooners come to Ann Arbor for one of the most anticipated games of the weekend.

Weather: 74 degrees, partly cloudy

All eyes will be on Underwood, even with Heisman-hopeful John Mateer on the other side. The tape from his performance last week has been highly scrutinized, and head coach Kyle Whittingham made some not-so-confident comments about him. The team as a whole was far from perfect, but Underwood's decision-making and inefficient play cost the team on numerous occasions.

Rewind 365 days ago, and the same could be said about Underwood making his first road start in Norman against a dominant Brent Venables-led defense. He was just 9-for-24 for 142 yards in a game where he didn't take as much heat because of the situation.

That won't be the case this year, and it's not just because he's a year older. It's also the supporting cast he has around him. That's highlighted by what appear to be star newcomers J.J. Buchanan and Savion Hiter, along with returners Andrew Marsh and Jordan Marshall, behind an improved offensive line. Michigan can no longer afford for its quarterback to be holding them back.

Michigan's defense was the main reason it ended up beating Western Michigan. One thing that will translate for Jay Hill and the unit heading into this game is preparing for Mateer's legs. The Wolverines held quarterback Broc Lowry and running back Jalen Buckley, two of the MAC's premier rushers, to only 2.4 yards per carry on 34 combined attempts.

They'll face an upgrade this weekend in Mateer and a running back-by-committee situation. Mateer ran the ball 19 times against Michigan last season for 74 yards, constantly keeping the Oklahoma offense on the field. If the Wolverines can slow him down, they should have a solid chance of containing the Sooners' offense.

Heading into last Saturday, Michigan was favored by 2.5 points. The near-loss to Western Michigan swung the spread all the way to 5.5 points in Oklahoma's favor. That feels right from a narrative perspective, but the bettor in me sees a pretty significant opportunity knowing this is also the Sooners' first road contest of the season. title: Arkansas at Utah Preview: Razorbacks Cannot Pretend Week One Was Enough
description: Arkansas at Utah is the first road game of the Ryan Silverfield era with a win. Still, the performance against North Alabama left too many unanswered questions to believe the Razorbacks are ready for Utah. With this, we at Last Word on College Football present the Arkansas and Utah preview. And the Razorbacks cannot pretend …
fullText:
Arkansas at Utah is the first road game of the Ryan Silverfield era with a win. Still, the performance against North Alabama left too many unanswered questions to believe the Razorbacks are ready for Utah. With this, we at Last Word on College Football present the Arkansas and Utah preview. And the Razorbacks cannot pretend the week one win was enough.

Arkansas is 1-0. That is the good news. The bad news is the Razorbacks did not look like a team ready to walk into Salt Lake City and beat Utah. Arkansas defeated North Alabama 31-14, outgaining the Lions 415-153 and holding the ball for more than 41 minutes. Those numbers should describe a comfortable, complete victory. Instead, the Razorbacks committed eight penalties, turned the ball over three times, averaged 3.0 yards per carry, and scored only one touchdown in six red-zone trips.

That is not a formula that travels. Utah is coming off a 66-14 win against Idaho in which it gained 633 yards, rushed for 364 yards, and did not allow a sack. Devon Dampier was efficient, Utah's running game was relentless, and the Utes did not need their starters to play under pressure for long. Arkansas will enter Saturday night as an underdog for a reason.

KJ Jackson was Arkansas' best offensive development in Week 1. He completed 24 of 35 passes for 267 yards, three touchdowns, and one interception. He spread the football around, showed poise after a difficult stretch before halftime, and made better decisions in the second half.

That is encouraging. It is not enough. Jackson also threw an interception and lost a fumble. Arkansas did not consistently threaten North Alabama vertically, allowing the Lions to keep defenders near the line of scrimmage and make the Razorbacks work for nearly every rushing yard.

Utah will take the same approach unless Jackson proves it cannot. The Razorbacks need Jackson to make better decisions, but they also need to help him. A quarterback cannot develop if every critical snap becomes third-and-eight. Arkansas must run the ball more effectively, protect better, and create throws that do not demand a perfect read against a ranked defense. Jackson can give Arkansas a chance. He cannot carry a one-dimensional offense for four quarters in a difficult road environment.

Arkansas rushed for 148 yards on 49 carries against North Alabama. That is 3.0 yards per attempt against an FCS opponent. There is no kind way to frame it: that is a warning sign. Sutton Smith gained 36 yards on 15 carries. Braylen Russell had 49 yards and a touchdown on 17 attempts. Neither runner found enough space to establish a consistent rhythm, and the offensive line did not create the movement Arkansas will need against Utah. The Razorbacks can talk about creativity, different personnel packages, and better execution. They should. But Saturday will reveal whether those are solutions or simply explanations.

If Arkansas cannot run against Utah, the rest of the game becomes predictable. Jackson faces more pressure. The Utes can sit on short routes. Arkansas becomes dependent on winning difficult one-on-one matchups outside. That is not an upset formula.

Arkansas limited North Alabama to 153 yards, but Utah demands a different standard. The Utes are built to stress every level of a defense. They can run the ball. They can throw it. Dampier can beat Arkansas when the original play breaks down.

The Razorbacks must tackle better than they did in the situations where North Alabama extended drives. They cannot lose edge containment. They cannot give Utah short fields after turnovers. And they cannot allow the Utes to build an early lead that turns Rice-Eccles Stadium into an even bigger factor.

Arkansas does not need to win the statistical battle against Utah's offense. It needs to avoid the avalanche. The defense must get off the field on third down, force at least one turnover, and make Utah settle for field goals rather than touchdowns. If the Utes reach 30 points, Arkansas has not shown enough offensive consistency to assume it can match them.

Arkansas can compete if it plays its cleanest game. That means no giveaways. It means fewer than eight penalties. It means Jackson taking care of the football, the offensive line creating a functional running game, and the defense containing Dampier rather than chasing him.

But based on Week 1, those are a lot of improvements to expect in one week. Utah has a more complete offense, an established quarterback, and home-field advantage. Arkansas has a talented young quarterback, but it also has a rushing attack that has not proven it can carry its share of the load and an offense that repeatedly squandered scoring chances against North Alabama. The Razorbacks can make this competitive. They should not be expected to win unless they play far better than they did in Week one.

Prediction: Utah 31, Arkansas 17

title: ESPN College GameDay is no longer appropriate for children, some parents say
description: Pat McAfee received criticism for cussing and encouraging fans to do so ahead of the LSU vs. Clemson game.
fullText:
ESPN College GameDay returned this past weekend to preview Week 1 of the college football season, including LSU's matchup against Clemson.

The three-hour show, which first aired in 1987, continues to be a popular way for college football fans to begin their Saturdays.

However, some believe ESPN star Pat McAfee is making the show no longer appropriate for kids.

McAfee encouraged LSU fans to sing "Neck" on multiple occasions Saturday morning. The song includes the lyrics "Suck that Tiger [expletive], [expletive]."

Some fans took to X and complained that they no longer feel like they can watch the show with their kids.

"Hey @CollegeGameDay can you tell Pat McAfee to watch his mouth? I could watch College Gameday with my kids until he came on. We just turned it off because he can't control his tongue… @espn @ESPNCFB @Disney," one post said.

Another added: "Honestly, I am just sick of hearing 'suck that Tiger [expletive] [expletive]' on a dang morning show. We all know they say it but why do we need to have it blasting at 10:45 am on national TV? My kids love watching College Gameday but man I hate that part every year when they're in BR."

As the show was kicking off, College GameDay posted a video of McAfee on X.

In the 32-second video, McAfee said, "Hello beautiful people. After a long, long offseason, College GameDay is all the way back from Baton Rouge, baby. ... It's hot as hell, the storylines are in abundance, and college football's about to showcase to the world why it's the greatest sport on earth. We start here at 9 a.m. Eastern on ESPN. ... Let's go."

The comments section was filled with complaints about McAfee and what the show has become.

"Impossible watch. Thank you for ruining something great," one fan said.

Another fan said, "Yeah, he's the reason that, after 28 years of Gameday being must see tv for me 3 hours every Saturday morning, I don't tune in anymore. His schtick was funny for about 10 minutes then it just got old."

McAfee clearly has a large following and is one of the biggest personalities in sports media.

The complaints, however, suggest a segment of the college football audience has grown frustrated with his presence on the show.

title: Gavin Newsom expresses 'openness' to packing SCOTUS, calls Electoral College system 'perverted'
description: Dem California Gov. Gavin Newsom said he was "evolving" on the idea of expanding the Supreme Court and eliminating the Electoral College during an interview Tuesday.
fullText:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom expressed "openness" to reforming the Supreme Court and claimed the Electoral College "perverted" politics during an interview with former CNN host Don Lemon on his podcast Tuesday.

Near the end of the interview, Lemon directly asked Newsom, a rumored 2028 candidate, whether he believed the judicial branch needed to be expanded, an idea pushed by several Democratic figures, including former Vice President Kamala Harris.

"My initial instinct — me, a year ago, I would have said no out of concern that it will continue to be expanded," Newsom said.

"And I was making a case for the ethical reforms and term limits, 18 years, which I was making a case a year ago. I'm more open to it on the basis of those district court arguments, which are not terrible arguments."

Democratic Senator Claims Gop 'Stole' Two Scotus Seats In 2016, 2020, Calls For Expansion

"I'm finding myself evolving on it. I normally have very clear conviction on things. I've been open to argument and interested in the evidence on this," Newsom answered.

He described his position as "caution on expanding it, but openness," adding that he believes reforms like term limits are a "no-brainer."

Harris Labeled 'Institutional Arsonist' For Plan To Fundamentally Transform Scotus And Electoral College

The California Democrat had harsher criticism of the Electoral College, suggesting that it has "perverted" U.S. politics.

"California has already been a leader that's already gone out front saying it's time to change that system. Which state's more burdened by it than my state? We're the size of 21 state populations combined. Come on. And we have two representatives in the Senate? Come on.

"And the way that thing favors ... it's perverted, I think, our politics. The Constitution is a living document, and it was conceived to be amended, and I think it's time to make that amendment," Newsom said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment.

Carville Tells Dems To Quietly Prepare Power Grab With Dc, Puerto Rico Statehood And Supreme Court Packing

Though Newsom has not explicitly supported expanding the Supreme Court, he made similar comments suggesting an openness to it during an interview with Brian Tyler Cohen on his podcast in June. Cohen was arguing in favor of court expansion, and Newsom remarked that Cohen was "getting me closer to your point of view."

During an interview with "PBS NewsHour" on Monday, Newsom also said the Democratic Party is "pretty aligned" with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) on issues like universal healthcare, climate change and moving off fossil fuels. The DSA's goals include eliminating the Supreme Court and replacing it with a judiciary that would be selected by Congress.

House Democrats recently voted against a constitutional amendment to cap the number of justices on the Supreme Court at nine. Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Ariz., who introduced the measure, warned Congress about the downsides of expanding the court.

"Here's the question every American should ask: If a sitting majority can change the size of the Supreme Court the moment it dislikes rulings, what happens to the next time the other side is in power?" Biggs said on the floor.

The entire college football world has been focused on the Michigan clock scandal in their victory over Western Michigan. Michigan would not have been in the situation to need a Hail Mary to win the game had Bryce Underwood played better. This has led to the possibility that Underwood could be benched by Michigan.

Now, comments about the backup quarterback Tommy Carr, made by Kyle Whittingham in the spring, are being looked at and could be hinting at a potential benching of Underwood, per Matt Hayes of USA Today.

"He's just got 'it.' You watch him play, and it's so obvious," Whittingham said in the spring about Carr. "He's young, he's a freshman. But he's a ball player."

title: Who will be 'College GameDay' guest picker for Texas-Ohio State? Potential Week 2 choices

fullText:
The college football world turns its attention to a matchup between top-three ranked teams when No. 3 Texas hosts No. 1 Ohio State in Week 2 with ESPN's "College GameDay" on deck.

It's the second matchup of a home-and-home series that started last season with Ohio State's 14-7 win in a low-scoring affair. Both Julian Sayin and Arch Manning made their debuts as full-time starters in the game, and have both blossomed into two of the best signal-callers in college football since their shaky starts.

Texas, of course, gives ESPN plenty of celebrities and former sports icons to choose from to be the celebrity guest picker. The second-largest school in Texas, the largest state in the continental United States, is not only one of the top public schools in the nation but also one of the most historically impressive in athletics.

Who will the celebrity guest picker be when "College GameDay" visits Austin, Texas? Here's a look at some potential options:

Academy Award-winning actor Matthew McConaughey is the obvious choice, almost never missing his alma mater's games. The football team's "minister of culture" also teaches a film class at Texas.

McConaughey is already also appearing in the media ahead of Texas-Ohio State, talking to Scott Van Pelt on ESPN's "SportsCenter" on Sept. 7. He already once appeared on "GameDay" back in 2019, but it seems about time for the fan favorite to come back on the show.

“It’s between the ears of more of these young men on this football team, the belief that this is the time to do it.”@McConaughey speaks with @notthefakeSVP about the expectations on Texas football and the team’s belief 🏈 pic.twitter.com/zS0eDjPJse

ESPN might want to include Arch Manning's dad, Cooper Manning, in the festivities, too — but getting Eli and Peyton Manning, who star in numerous ESPN productions alongside each other, would be a huge hit among fans.

Former Texas star Vince Young led the Longhorns to their most recent national championship in 2005 after scoring one of the most iconic touchdowns in college football history. Young has never been the guest picker on "College GameDay," but he would be a smart choice by the pregame show, given his legendary status in Texas' history.

Kevin Durant only spent one season at Texas, but it might've been the school's single-best campaign in program history. The NBA legend has never been shy of boasting his Texas fandom, and he would be a nice get for "College GameDay."

Scottie Scheffler is the No. 1-ranked golfer in the world, and just so happened to attend Texas. The Texas native might not be the likeliest choice since he appeared on the show in 2024, but he's a very relevant sports icon connected to the school.

Scheffler has 22 career PGA Tour wins, two of which were Masters Tournament victories in 2022 and 2024.

title: Colorado TPUSA chapter enrollment 'flat' after elderly supporter was struck by student with Taco Bell cup
description: Video captured the chaos after Fort Lewis College approved a Turning Point USA chapter, but nearly a year later, membership remains stagnant.
fullText:
Enrollment at the Turning Point USA (TPUSA) chapter at Fort Lewis College in Durango, Colorado, remains flat due to students' fears of retaliation, according to chapter leaders and local supporters. The stagnation comes nearly a year after the campus group's registration sparked intense pushback from the surrounding community and student body.

"It's definitely been flat, I would say," Rachel Cook, vice president of the Fort Lewis College chapter, told Fox News Digital.

Cook's comments come nearly a year after the student government's decision to recognize the chapter touched off severe turmoil on campus — much of which was captured on video and obtained by Fox News Digital.

Erika Kirk Urges Conservative Students Not To Back Down In First School Year Since Charlie's Assassination

One video showed a student being detained by campus police after striking 66-year-old local resident David Peters with a Taco Bell cup outside the student senate chambers.

Peters, former chair of the La Plata County GOP and a retired Chevron executive, reflected on the incident and its lingering effect on the student group.

"Their membership has been essentially flat. The issue is that a lot of students are reluctant to join the chapter for fear of retaliation," Peters said. "And their fears are well-founded. There have been some members who have received anonymous death threats."

Cook echoed those safety concerns.

"One of the main things is that students have said they are hesitant to join because of their personal safety. A lot of our officers have been getting threats and being harassed," she said.

Uc Berkeley Sued For Allegedly Stonewalling Probe Into Violent Ambush At Tpusa Rob Schneider Event

The tensions at Fort Lewis College unfolded amid a national surge in interest for TPUSA campus chapters. Following the September 10, 2025, assassination of TPUSA co-founder Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University, the conservative organization reported receiving more than 120,000 inquiries from students seeking to establish local chapters.

At Fort Lewis College, then-senior Jonah Flynn led the effort to establish a presence on campus. Although the Associated Students of Fort Lewis College (ASFLC) initially rejected Flynn's proposal, the student government ultimately reversed course and voted to approve the group during an emergency session.

The vote prompted immediate outrage from anti-TPUSA spectators waiting outside the meeting room.

According to a Fort Lewis College campus police report, approximately 70 people attended the high-tension meeting. As attendees spilled out into the lobby, an argument broke out between attendees holding opposing views.

The police report states that Peters approached a student who was "booing and yelling" while holding his phone about a foot away to record. title: LSU announces final decision on adding former NFL players
description: The biggest storyline in college football over the past few weeks has been LSU and head coach Lane Kiffin’s attempts to add multiple players to its roster who had signed NFL contracts and spent time with NFL teams this preseason. Now, LSU has made a final decision on that matter. With the looming threat of…
fullText:
The biggest storyline in college football over the past few weeks has been LSU and head coach Lane Kiffin's attempts to add multiple players to its roster who had signed NFL contracts and spent time with NFL teams this preseason. Now, LSU has made a final decision on that matter.

With the looming threat of expulsion from the SEC, the Tigers have made it clear that they will not add the players to the roster this season.

Heading into the 2026 season, LSU and Kiffin had been moving forward with plans to bring in at least three players who signed professional contracts this summer, including former Ole Miss players Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris.

Adding those players to the roster would break two separate league rules, as the SEC prohibits players from entering the conference after signing a professional contract while also restricting intraconference transfers outside of the designated transfer portal window.

However, a Baton Rouge judge has issued an order preventing both the NCAA and SEC from enforcing their restrictions related to eligibility, the transfer portal, and professional players returning to college football.

On Thursday last week, Judge William Jorden, out of Baton Rouge, Louisiana, ruled in favor of LSU by approving a preliminary injunction "that prohibits the NCAA and SEC from punishing any school" that fields former professional players. That would have paved the way for the players to potentially play in Saturday's game against Clemson.

Ultimately, LSU opted against adding the players to the roster for this game. However, the team only rostered 103 players for the game, allowing two open spots to potentially add Wright and Harris to the roster later in the season.

According to college football insider Pete Thamel of ESPN, LSU has announced a final decision on the matter by adding two additional players to the school's roster. This means that the team's roster is now full at 105 players, and Wright and Harris will not be able to be added to the roster this season.

"NEWS: LSU football is adding two players to the school's roster, which will complete it at 105 players, per ESPN sources. This will lock LSU's roster for the rest of the year, which will eliminate the program's ability to add Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris," Thamel wrote in a post on X.

This should seemingly bring the whole ordeal to a close.

title: LSU locks roster, Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris will not play for the Tigers
description: Wright and Harris were both on rosters during the NFL preseason, and their potential return to college football sparked plenty of controversy.
fullText:
The battle over former NFL players returning to college appears to be over, for now.

LSU has added two players to its roster, bringing the total to 105 players. The Tigers added DE Gabriel Reliford and CB Aidan Anding, per Yahoo Sports' Ross Dellenger.

With the roster at 105 players, neither Dae'Quan Wright nor Zxavian Harris will be allowed to join the LSU roster this season.

Wright and Harris have been in the media and the subject of plenty of discussion because both of them participated in this year's NFL preseason, going so far as to suit up for preseason games.

After not making their respective NFL rosters, and after the NCAA passed a new eligibility rule allowing players five years of eligibility over five years, both Wright and Harris were looking to return to the college ranks for one more season.

Lawyers got involved, and different injunctions were permitted in different states, and the situation got extremely confusing and murky very quickly.

This sparked plenty of controversy among FBS teams, culminating in the SEC and LSU scheduling court dates and meetings to discuss what could be done to the school should it add pro players. One outcome included the conference removing LSU as a member school, but that may have been avoided.

While this seems like it was a big threat from the SEC, Dellenger reported that if the vote had passed and been enacted immediately, next week's highly anticipated game between Ole Miss and LSU would have suddenly been a non-conference game.

At this time, it has not been reported whether Thursday's scheduled meeting to "decide whether to terminate Louisiana State University ('LSU') as an SEC member institution" has been canceled or if it will still be held.

Wright and Harris were ruled eligible ahead of LSU's season-opening game against Clemson. Both players were with new head coach Lane Kiffin at Ole Miss, but Kiffin opted not to add them to the roster at the time, leaving two spots open out of a maximum of 105.

The LSU head coach spoke about the decision during an appearance on "College GameDay," mainly attributing it to the fact that they didn't yet know what a punishment, if any, would look like for the program.

"That wasn't easy. As much as I feel for the players, and I believe that you fight for what you believe in, and I believe that, you know, these kids have an opportunity to play, just like all of the other kids around the country that are winning court cases and being put on rosters.

But the same time, I'm the head coach at LSU and I had to make a decision that is for the big picture of LSU and the LSU football program, with the uncertainties of what potentially could've come by adding them to the roster."

"That wasn't easy. As much as I feel for the players ... I had to make a decision that is for the big picture of LSU."

Lane Kiffin on the decision to not roster Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris for today's game against Clemson. pic.twitter.com/iPVHJTYoav

Now with its roster officially set, LSU will look to continue the momentum generated with a Week 1 dominant 51-10 win over Clemson.

title: NHL Prospect Who Collapsed During College Workout Suffered Heat Stroke and Lost Oxygen to Brain: ‘We Need a Miracle’
description: Matthew Mayich collapsed during an outdoor workout on Aug. 20 in Arizona
fullText:
NHL prospect Matthew Mayich suffered a heat stroke and lost oxygen to his brain during the workout at Arizona State University on Aug. 20, his family's attorney said

"There were no other contributing conditions, only exertion-related heat," the attorney said, adding, "We need a miracle"

Mayich collapsed during an outdoor workout in extreme Arizona heat where he was reportedly given "minimal water"

NHL prospect Matthew Mayich suffered a heat stroke and lost oxygen to his brain when he collapsed during a military-style outdoor workout, according to his family's lawyer.

Rob Carey, the attorney representing the family of the 21-year-old Arizona State University hockey player who was drafted by the St. Louis Blues, told ESPN, "This injury is from exertional heat stroke that caused a lack of oxygen to the brain."

"There were no other contributing conditions, only exertion-related heat. This is not an induced coma," Carey told the outlet, adding, "We need a miracle."

The attorney emphasized in his statement to ESPN that Mayich "didn't last one day" after his arrival to ASU and said the Aug. 20 workout when he collapsed "was the first day of coach-led practice."

Mayich remains in the hospital with "zero chance of recovery," Mayich previously told the Arizona Republic.

The workout was reportedly led by a former military service member who had volunteered to lead the team's exercises, per NBC affiliate 12 News.

Carey told ESPN that Mayich became disoriented and dizzy in the moments before he collapsed on the track. The athlete was also given "minimal water" during the workout, which took place while Arizona was under an extreme heat warning, according to a local weather report.

The Sun Devils turned off their comments on Instagram, and only one reply remains visible on X, which reads, "About 2 weeks too late…."

title: Week 2 college football betting, odds: 3 early bets to make right now
description: Our college football handicapper gives three early Week 2 wagers he likes.
fullText:
A year ago, Western Michigan walked into a Big Ten stadium in the first week of the season and turned the afternoon into a rock fight. Michigan State couldn't score. The total closed at 50 and the game produced 29 points. Then the Spartans beat Boston College 42-40 the following week.

That is the trade this week: One weekend into the season we have the loudest information grab the market gets all year, and it arrives with almost nothing to weigh it against. A team looks broken for three hours, everyone adjusts and the next number is set by an audience that has watched one game and remembered all of it. The interesting question is whether that adjustment is correct, and you can measure it.

Upgrade to Fantasy Plus and gain your edge in player projections and much more

Since 2016, there have been 241 cases of a team whose Week 1 game finished 14 or more points under its closing total; their Week 2 games went over 143 of those 241 times, a shade under 60%, with a median landing nearly three points clear of the number. The baseline for every Week 2 game total in that span is 49.7 percent.

I am hunting early bets on market overreactions headed into Week 2.

Michigan beat Western Michigan 13-12 in Ann Arbor on Saturday night. The total closed at 46.5 and the game produced 25 points. Same opponent, same conference, same ugly first Saturday that Michigan State had a year ago, and the market has responded the same way: this total opened at 46.5 and now sits at 43.5.

Three points is a lot. It is also a strange three points, because the offense that will decide this game had nothing to do with the afternoon that moved it. Oklahoma hung an easy 51 on UTEP, with quarterback John Mateer throwing for 225 yards and three scores before the backups came on in the third quarter. That offense has plenty of big-play ability, and if Michigan has a shot to stay in this one it's going to have to match some form of production. We make this total 49.8 points, split between Oklahoma 27.3 and Michigan 22.5.

There is a case against the over and it is tempo. Michigan grinds, Oklahoma is not much quicker and fewer possessions is a genuine headwind. But after what happened in Week 1, Michigan's offense could certainly use a 180-degree approach and play with more tempo than we saw.

Bet: Oklahoma-Michigan over 43.5 (-103)

Georgia Tech lost 14-13 to Colorado. Their total closed at 51.5 and the game delivered 27 points. Another "oh boy, should we worry?" from a Georgia Tech offense that had offseason hype. I am not selling just yet.

Look at how that game actually ended: Colorado scored with 42 seconds left, and Georgia Tech answered by moving into field-goal range before a 45-yard FG attempt was blocked. That is a coin flip, not a collapse. Alberto Mendoza, in his first start after transferring in from Indiana, went 17-of-23 for 237 yards.

Our projection is 62.5 points in this one(Tennessee 34.5 and Georgia Tech 28.0). Tennessee's offense was never in question, so nothing on that half of the ledger got marked down, which leaves Georgia Tech's 13-point afternoon carrying the entire adjustment by itself and asks you to believe that a team the market still respects enough to make only a 13-point home underdog has simultaneously forgotten how to score. Those two things are hard to hold at once.

I'm not running to tell you Colorado's defense is good and Georgia Tech deserves leeway, but it's Week 1 with a new quarterback. In a fight against Tennessee you have to be ready for big plays, and the Week 1 reaction opened value for us on the over.

Bet: Tennessee-Georgia Tech over 55.5 (+106)

Boise State went to Eugene and lost 34-27 in one of the most impressive opening performances of the year, and this is the spot where I do the opposite of the last two games: I am buying on the assumption the market didn't move enough.

The Broncos were 24.5-point underdogs and lost by seven. Oregon opened the season ranked second in the country with the second-shortest national title odds on the board at +650, and Boise went shot for shot with them in their building. The eye test and the number agree: this team is legit.

On the other side, Memphis has played twice — opening by winning outright at UNLV as a 4.5-point underdog and then beating Arkansas State 42-24 as a 10-point favorite — and while both of those are covers, the second is the narrower one, which is the sort of quiet step backward that tells me the market may have bought the hype a shade faster than the team earned it. Two games in also starts to add up in the fatigue department. That is not the state I want to be in walking into Boise.

The argument against Boise State if that if the Broncos had played worse you would be getting them under a touchdown here, so I am buying a relative high on a great performance. From everything I have seen, though, I believe it is well worth the buy on the Broncos.

title: High school QBs face new reality as transfers dominate starting jobs at the top of college football
description: Even though he was nearly 2,000 miles from where he'd grown up, Ryan Hopkins felt right at home as a quarterback prospect visiting Wisconsin.  Hopkins had to deal with the dilemma facing just about every high school quarterback prospect since most Bowl Subdivision programs now overwhemingly rely on transfers at that position: About 65% of the FBS starting quarterbacks to open this season transferred at some point in their careers.  “It’s a totally different ballgame,” said Trent Dilfer, who has experienced quarterback recruiting from just about every angle.
fullText:
MADISON, Wis. (AP) — Even though he was nearly 2,000 miles from where he'd grown up, Ryan Hopkins felt right at home as a quarterback prospect visiting Wisconsin.

"I felt the energy from the city," said Hopkins, a former three-star recruit from Mater Dei in Santa Ana, California. "I felt the energy from the coaches."

But there was a complication that went beyond the distance factor. Hopkins had to deal with the dilemma facing just about every high school quarterback prospect since most Bowl Subdivision programs now overwhemingly rely on transfers at that position: About 65% of the FBS starting quarterbacks to open this season transferred at some point in their careers.

"It's a totally different ballgame," said Trent Dilfer, who has experienced quarterback recruiting from just about every angle.

Dilfer is a former Fresno State quarterback and first-round draft pick who started for the Baltimore Ravens' Super Bowl championship team in the 2000 season. He coached a high school power at Lipscomb Academy in Nashville, Tennessee, was a college head coach at UAB and now is back at Lipscomb.

He remembers when a quarterback coming out of high school could learn on the job. Colleges don't need to be that patient anymore because so many college quarterbacks with starting experience are available each year since the NCAA erased the requirement of sitting out a year before the 2021-22 season.

"And that changed everything," Dilfer said. "Because instead of recruiting the child, now you're recruiting a man."

Hopkins chose Wisconsin even as the Badgers enter a fourth straight season with a transfer as their starting quarterback. Hopkins spent the summer competing with Louisville transfer Deuce Adams for the right to back up Old Dominion transfer Colton Joseph, who got the start in the Badgers' season-opening loss to No. 4 Notre Dame on Sunday night.

"I feel like with this coaching staff – no matter if you're the 2 or the 3 or the 1 - they're coaching every guy the same," Hopkins said.

The reliance on transfers by most major programs leaves fewer roster spots available for high school prospects.

"If you're a quarterback in this day and age, you have to earn it and you have to say, 'I'm OK with taking less when I'm first getting recruited, because I want to get more when I show how good I am,'" Washington coach Jedd Fisch said.

They also must realize the college they select out of high school might not be where they finish.

Going by composite rankings of recruiting sites compiled by 247Sports, more than 80% of the top 50 quarterbacks from the 2023 class have transferred. The number of top-50 quarterbacks from that class who have attended at least three colleges is nearly double the total who stayed at one school.

"A kid who used to be able to go to a middle-of-the-road SEC or ACC school, it's probably better for them to go now to a Group of Five school and play," said Bryant Appling, who coaches Georgia high school power Buford. "Because two years from now, when they want to transfer or move up, they'll have a leg up on the kid who's just coming out of high school and who they're not sure of."

All that activity makes it tough for high school quarterbacks who sign with colleges in December, just before the transfer portal window opens. Most finalize their college plans several months before that December deadline, when they have no idea who they might be competing against once they've enrolled.

"You're fishing in the dark, so to speak," said Jason Negro, the coach at St. John Bosco in Bellflower, California, whose list of former quarterbacks includes Illinois' Katin Houser and 2018 first-round pick Josh Rosen. "You have no control over it. You might look at a roster in November or December - and in January it looks completely different."

College coaches won't stop recruiting high school quarterbacks entirely, since they'd prefer to develop multi-year starters rather than depending on the portal each year. But the portal enables them to be choosier.

"If you're going to invest in somebody to play at this level, they'd better be able to play in year one or at least year two," Wisconsin coach Luke Fickell said.

Coaches also rarely sign multiple high school quarterbacks in the same class anymore. Rutgers coach Greg Schiano noted that "back in the day, if you were a little bit low in that room, you wouldn't think twice about doing that."

Some quarterbacks have been proactive by reclassifying to enter college a year early, enabling them to profit off the use their name, image and likeness sooner.

Teddy Jarrard is at Notre Dame this year rather than playing his senior season at North Cobb High School in Kennesaw, Georgia. Notre Dame also has a verbal commitment from Champ Monds, who skipped his junior season at Vero Beach (Florida) High and will begin his college career next year. Colorado's Julian Lewis also reclassified.

"Some guys are ready to do that," Schiano said. "They're physically mature enough. They're emotionally mature enough. Other guys, not even close."

While the transfer portal hinders high school quarterback prospects initially, it offers potential long-term benefits. Quarterbacks not recruited heavily in high school can work their way up.

"If they just get in there and play, even at the I-AA level, you've seen guys who have made big strides come up," Duke coach Manny Diaz said. "We've seen D-II guys that in the past might've just been stuck there forever and no one would have ever known about them."

Diego Pavia went from New Mexico Military Institute to New Mexico State to Vanderbilt and became the 2025 Heisman Trophy runner-up. Trinidad Chambliss started out at Division II Ferris State, led Mississippi to a College Football Playoff semifinal berth last year and is back behind center for the Rebels this season.

Chambliss is one of at least 18 FBS starting quarterbacks this season who spent part of their careers at non-FBS programs.

"I have a really good friend whose son is a really great quarterback and is asking where he should go," Nebraska coach Matt Rhule said. "I was like, 'I'd go to the place where I could start. I'd go FCS. I'd go wherever and play,' because everyone's going to want to see a quarterback with experience."

Chris McDonald, who coached Washington's Demond Williams and Oklahoma State's Broderick Vehrs at Basha High in Chandler, Arizona, said quarterbacks are now similar to baseball prospects moving up a farm system. Productive quarterbacks at lower-level schools get opportunities at bigger programs.

"Understand your recruitment really doesn't end until you're going into your last year of college," McDonald said.

Hopkins, the Wisconsin quarterback, offers this advice to high school QB recruits.

"Trust your development," he said. "Your development's huge. I think a lot of kids, they're really eager and they want to go to these really flashy programs because these coaches are throwing a lot at them. See yourself, be self-aware of your talents and what you're capable of."

AP sports writers Aaron Beard and Stephen Hawkins contributed to this report.

title: Ole Miss QB Trinidad Chambliss passes for 336 yards, runs for 60 in 41-38 win in opener
description: Ole Miss quarterback Trinidad Chambliss, who may prove to be among the most polarizing prospects in the 2027 NFL draft, is off to a good start to his final season of college football.
fullText:
Ole Miss quarterback Trinidad Chambliss, who may prove to be among the most polarizing prospects in the 2027 NFL draft, is off to a good start to his final season of college football.

Chambliss completed 21 of 36 passes for 336 yards, with three touchdowns and one interception, and also added nine carries for 60 yards and a rushing touchdown, as No. 9 Ole Miss beat No. 24 Louisville 41-38.

A year ago, Chambliss was a little-known transfer from Division II Ferris State who wasn't even expected to start at Ole Miss, but he became more than just a starter. He became one of the best players in the country, leading Ole Miss to the College Football Playoff.

So why is Chambliss polarizing as a prospect? He's on the smaller side (listed at 6-foot-1, possibly shorter) and is already 24 years old and in his sixth year of college football, so he may have less less upside and room for growth than some of the younger, less experienced quarterback projects.

Will Chambliss be a first-round pick? A Day Three pick? There's a wide range of potential outcomes, but he can help his case by continuing to play like he did against Louisville.

title: What Lane Kiffin said about being hated after LSU’s 51-10 win over Clemson
description: LSU spent the week before its opener in a Louisiana courtroom and in an exchange of statements with the SEC over the eligibility of former NFL players on college rosters. Lane Kiffin’s first team then beat Clemson 51-10 in Baton Rouge on Saturday night, and he brought the argument up himself at halftime. With LSU […] The post What Lane Kiffin said about being hated after LSU’s 51-10 win over Clemson appeared first on Gridiron Heroics.
fullText:
LSU spent the week before its opener in a Louisiana courtroom and in an exchange of statements with the SEC over the eligibility of former NFL players on college rosters. Lane Kiffin's first team then beat Clemson 51-10 in Baton Rouge on Saturday night, and he brought the argument up himself at halftime.

With LSU ahead 31-3 and holding a 336-54 edge in total yards at the break, Kiffin finished his interview with ESPN's Holly Rowe, started to walk away, then came back to the microphone and said, "Imagine if we had pro players."

Two days earlier, East Baton Rouge Parish Judge William Jorden granted a preliminary injunction barring the NCAA and the SEC from punishing schools that rostered any of the 42 athletes suing for a fifth season of eligibility, which cleared former Ole Miss players Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris to follow Kiffin to Baton Rouge. The SEC filed its own federal lawsuit against LSU and Kiffin in Alabama that same morning. LSU submitted a 103-man roster on Friday and left the two spots empty.

Kiffin explained that decision on ESPN's "College GameDay" hours before kickoff.

"That wasn't easy, as much as I feel for the players," he said. "And I believe that you fight for what you believe in. And I believe these kids have an opportunity to play, just like all the other kids around the country that are winning court cases and being put on rosters. title: What Utah Tech coach Lance Anderson said after losing to BYU
description: Upon falling 63-7 to BYU Saturday night in Provo, Utah Tech head coach Lance Anderson has a better understanding of why so many people have projected the Cougars to be a potential College Football Playoff squad.  With the loss, Utah Tech falls to 0-2 on the season, having been defeated 54-0 by defending FCS national champion Montana State this past week.
fullText:
Upon falling 63-7 to BYU Saturday night in Provo, Utah Tech head coach Lance Anderson has a better understanding of why so many people have projected the Cougars to be a potential College Football Playoff squad.

"Obviously it's hard to say after one game, and obviously we did not match up real well with them, but you look at their roster and I think they got a lot of those (championship caliber) pieces," Anderson told reporters postgame.

"Especially if some of these young receivers continue to come through, because I think it starts with the quarterback. You've got an outstanding running back in L.J. Martin ... great kid. They're physical up front on both sides of the ball, offensive line, defensive line. I think they've got some very athletic players in that linebacker room and DB room. So I think they've got the pieces in place. I think it'll be interesting to see how the year plays out."

Anderson, a longtime Stanford assistant, knows BYU's Kalani Sitake well, having faced off both in the Pac-12 and FCS ranks prior to Saturday. Anderson's daughter even worked for Sitake during her schooling at BYU.

"I think what's made him so successful is he understands BYU well," Anderson said of Sitake. "Being here as a player, being here as a coach, I think he understands this place and what it's about and what it represents. He's done a great job of building this (program), I think he's done it his way with his personality. That, I think, leads to that sustained and long-term success."

Anderson is also well-acquainted with new Cougars defensive coordinator Kelly Poppinga, whose starters impressed on Saturday before the backups surrendered a lone fourth quarter touchdown.

"I think he's an outstanding football coach," Anderson said of Poppinga. "You look at the film from last year, the last couple years with Jay Hill as a defensive coordinator, I think they've got a very good system and they've not really strayed far from that. We could see that tonight, but I think Kelly's brought a few wrinkles of his own from his time with Bronco Mendenhall and his coaching experience. I think he'll do a phenomenal job as a defensive coordinator.

"... I think BYU's got a great team, and I think they're going to be very successful this year."

With the loss, Utah Tech falls to 0-2 on the season, having been defeated 54-0 by defending FCS national champion Montana State this past week.

Anderson's Trailblazers, picked to finish last in the Big Sky Conference, will continue their early gauntlet in visiting heavily-favored Montana next week.

"I think games like this are fun opportunities," Anderson said. "Opening the season against the No. 1 FCS team in the country, Montana State, that's a great challenge. Being able to play in this environment at BYU today, great, great opportunity.

"We get a chance to go to Montana next week, which is another tremendous place to play, where that place is gonna be packed, it's gonna be loud. Fans are right on top of you. So our guys are excited about this, they're gonna go out and compete."

fullText:
Texas A&M kicked off the 2026 regular season against Missouri State on Saturday night, and while starting the season off 1-0 was fully expected, one of third-year coach Mike Elko's remaining challenges that has haunted the program for 20-plus seasons resurfaced this week before the season opener, as ESPN's College GameDay's nine appearances in College Station have been disastrous.

Since 2000, Texas A&M is just 1-8 when College GameDay made its way to College Station, with the first loss coming against No. 1 Oklahoma 35-31, while the only win came during the 2016 season when the Aggies defeated visiting Tennessee 45-38 in double overtime, which happens to be one of the most exciting finishes in recent memory.

Since that victory, the Jimbo Fisher era has been equally disappointing after six seasons, while the lone College GameDay loss to Clemson during Fisher's first season at the helm was a game that could, and should have, gone the other way if it weren't for several avoidable performances.

During Mike Elko's inaugural season, Texas A&M's loss to rival Texas at the end of the 2024 season wasn't a shock given the talent differential, while the Aggies' first-round loss to Miami in the first round of the College Football Playoff was by far the most disappointing defeat with College GameDay in town.

When the lights are brightest, Texas A&M must respond if the Aggies want to be taken seriously as a program truly building and contending for national titles, and while the 2025 season was certainly a solid start, expectations are even higher in 2026. If College GameDay makes its way back to College Station, it's time to change the narrative.

title: Emotional Taylor steps on to the scales one final time
description: Katie Taylor and Flora Pili weigh in under the light-welterweight limit at a sun-kissed Trinity College in Dublin before they fight for the undisputed title at Croke Park on Saturday.
fullText:
Katie Taylor has taken her final week as a professional boxer in her stride.

Each media event has been ticked off with the kind of composure and poise she has displayed in the ring for over two decades.

Dublin blessed Taylor and opponent Flora Pili with some early autumn sun as they weighed in at Trinity College before Saturday's undisputed light-welterweight battle at a sold-out Croke Park.

Taylor has not missed weight once in her 26-fight career and she was not going to buck the trend as she was greeted by adoring fans - many whom have followed her career since she won Olympic gold in 2012.

The announcement of the weights - both coming in just under the 10st (63.5kg) limit - was almost immaterial.

All 80,000 tickets for Saturday's undisputed light-welterweight fight have been long snapped up and demand for Friday's ceremonial weigh-in proved just as high.

Supporters packed into Trinity College, a seat of higher learning founded in 1592 by Queen Elizabeth I, to catch a glimpse of the queen of Irish sport.

Women were not permitted to study at Trinity College until 1975 but Taylor, who has smashed barriers for women in and out of the ring - was the star attraction.

Trinity's old library is an attraction in its own right, home to the Book of Kells - an illustrated manuscript, which contains the four Gospels of the New Testament in Latin - but those in its grounds were there for their own piece of history on this final fight week of Taylor's illustrious career.

The 40-year-old, two-weight undisputed champion, may not be a huge fan of the fight week obligations and making weight is certainly an aspect to the sport that will not be missed, but this was an opportunity to soak it all in one last time.

Pili has been the perfect guest all week, complimentary and polite, but the Frenchwoman is not here to be a tourist and there was an air of confidence as she hit the scales.

The 29-year-old has stitched together a perfect record of 12 wins and has an opportunity to raise her own reputation if she can pull of a major upset.

It is Pili's biggest night, an opportunity to catapult herself into the upper echelons of the fight game, but an also occasion she has never experienced and looked a little bemused as she stepped on to the scales.

As violinists played Irish folk song 'Óró, sé do bheatha 'bhaile' [Óró - you are welcome home], Taylor appeared to a rapturous reception and the fighters went through the formalities, all smiles and handshakes.

Tears and tricolours - inside Irish icon Taylor's final fight week

'Dear Katie, how far we have come...' - Taylor gets reply from her hero

Five moments that shaped Taylor's legendary career

Taylor rarely displays emotion in fight week but she has shown a different side of the past couple of days as the curtain starts to fall on her illustrious career.

The Bray fighter, who had her mother Bridgit close by, choked up at times and appeared as she delivered her final messages.

"I'm so excited. I've been saying all week how I grateful I am for this opportunity. I've been dreaming of this for the last few years and now it's just one day away. It's just one day away from ending my career in my dream venue of Croke Park," Taylor told the crowd after her final face-off.

"All these amazing people are here today and I'm blown away. I can't wait to step in there and I want to put in a performance worthy of everyone's support.

"You have carried me through the Rio Olympics, London Olympics and throughout my professional career. Thank you."

Both fighters can now breathe a little easier as it is onto the task at hand.

The buzz that has steadily built all week will reach a crescendo when they make their way to the ring around 22:00 BST on Saturday, and while the occasion remains grand, the destination of the title belts remains the priority.

"My mind is very much focused on the fight," Taylor reiterated.

"I have a tough challenger in front of me but I've built a reputation of taking tough fights - why treat my last fight any differently?

"Tomorrow is going to be an amazing celebration. I'm super proud to represent this amazing country. Let's go one more time."

fullText:
Ukrainian Kate Koval says she left Louisiana State University's basketball program because of the team's decision to sign a Russian player.

Following the arrival of Anna Minaeva, it was announced that 20-year-old Koval had departed for "personal reasons" after one season.

Koval said Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine was why she stepped away.

"My father serves in the Ukrainian military and takes tremendous pride in defending his country against Russian aggression," she wrote on Instagram.

"For me, this war is not distant or abstract. People close to me have been killed and wounded in Russian attacks, and places where I grew up and first began playing basketball have been destroyed by missile strikes.

"The timing of this situation and the deep personal effect it has had on me, my family and those we care about who continue to live through and fight this war ultimately made me question whether LSU remained the right place for me.

"This decision has not been easy. While I understand and respect that roster decisions are a part of college basketball, I have to remain true to myself, my values and my country."

Koval, who was expected to be LSU's starting centre this year, has two years of collegiate eligibility remaining.

The transfer portal has closed, but she said she hopes the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) "recognises the circumstances surrounding my situation and understands the seriousness and deep nature of this matter" and allows her to join a different university for the upcoming season.

Koval said: "I felt I had found a home at LSU, and I am incredibly grateful for my team-mates who became family, as well as my coaches, staff, professors and the entire LSU community.

"I will always cherish the relationships, experiences, and memories I made there."

title: Louisiana Judge Rules Players Can Go From NFL Back to College
description: The ruling allows players to go from the NFL to college rosters.
fullText:
LSU and Lane Kiffin are victorious—for now.

On Thursday evening in a courthouse in Baton Rouge, Judge William Jorden issued a ruling that extends legal protections for several football players seeking to go from the NFL preseason back to college rosters.

The ruling applies to dozens of players across multiple sports, and challenges the implementation of the NCAA's new age-based eligibility rule, rather than focusing on professional participation. It has sweeping implications, notably allowing players who have played in NFL preseason to sign with college rosters for the first time.

In the wake of the landmark decision, the most immediate question was whether some of the athletes in the case would appear in games—including Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, who had signed NFL contracts but have since secured deals to play for LSU this season. LSU will have to make that choice, but has previously signalled they would roster these athletes if given the chance.

Those players are now protected by a court order.

The next question: whether the SEC and NCAA would be legally allowed to penalize LSU under the court's order. LSU is now protected, as Jorden entered a specification protecting the school from sanctions coming from the NCAA or SEC.

The case also raised an existential question: whether the SEC has the power as a conference to enforce its rules, especially in a legal environment where the NCAA is regularly sued. That last question wasn't answered by the ruling Thursday night.

The conference also filed a separate lawsuit of its own in Alabama federal court against LSU, Kiffin, and athletic director Verge Ausberry. With echoes of the Big 12's case against Texas Tech over Brendan Sorsby, the SEC is seeking a federal ruling that would ensure it could prevent LSU from playing these athletes.

The SEC is likely to continue proceedings in that case, especially if LSU rosters Harris and Wright for Saturday's game.

The landmark decision ends a contentious day in Baton Rouge, after several hours of oral arguments, including three hours of questioning for SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey, according to those present in the courtroom and reportedly left through a side door due to security concerns.

A web of elected officials either participated or looked on in person and from afar, including Louisiana attorney general Liz Murrill, who filed a brief in support of players and attended the proceedings. During the testimony, she singled out Dae'Quan Wright, saying, "Dae'Quan Wright, who played for Ole Miss, says he lost out on seven-figure NIL money in a fifth year. Mississippi didn't fight for him, but Louisiana will."

The legal battle didn't originate as one over former NFL players, however. The first Louisiana state case was one of many filed against the NCAA challenging the implementation of its new "age-based eligibility policy." The new rules allow players five seasons of eligibility—but the NCAA said it would not extend this new policy to players who started college in 2022 and had already exhausted four years of eligibility.

The players who filed the Louisiana suit were part of this group, but the case drew ire because some of the athletes had signed NFL contracts (even preseason deals) and been listed on NFL rosters. After Judge Jorden issued a temporary restraining order in favor of the players, LSU scooped up two of them: Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris.

In response, the SEC (as well as other conferences) released a policy banning players with NFL preseason experience. Neither the players nor LSU appeared to back down, however: Kiffin allowed Wright to join LSU practices earlier this week, while players' attorneys got the SEC added to the temporary restraining order.

Because of the SEC's lawsuit, the drama is likely only beginning. The case argues that the SEC would be harmed if LSU rosters players with NFL preseason experience or who signed NFL contracts, and asks a judge to "enter a preliminary and permanent injunction prohibiting Defendants from violating the Conference's First Amendment rights by compelling the Conference to associate with conduct that is contrary to the Conference's purpose and mission."

Attorneys for the SEC and/or NCAA are expected to file immediate appeals of Jorden's injunction in the hopes that it could be at least paused before Saturday.

LSU's roster for the season is due to be finalized on Friday. On Saturday, the Tigers will finally take the field against Clemson for the most highly anticipated team debut of the year.

Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry declared in a celebratory post on X/Twitter after the ruling: "Let's spot the ball! #GeauxTigers!"

title: An Ohio college student died in an apparent suicide. His family says he felt ‘humiliated’ by his ICE ankle monitor
description: Pierre Damas Bel was killed Monday after he stepped into traffic on Interstate 70 near Springfield, Ohio. The Haitian immigrant’s family says he was distraught over being bullied for wearing an ICE an...
fullText:
EDITOR'S NOTE:  This story involves discussion of suicide that some readers may find upsetting. If you feel you are in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the 24-hour Suicide Crisis Lifeline.

Pierre Damas Bel was an avid soccer player at his high school in Springfield, Ohio. He loved being part of JROTC, the US military-sponsored program that provides training to students. And friends and family say he headed to college planning to study neuroscience and excited about the future.

But as the 20-year-old Haitian immigrant began his freshman year at Wright State University, his loved ones say he became increasingly depressed over the ankle monitor he was issued in late July by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The device, they say, sidelined him from playing soccer, stopped him from getting a new ROTC uniform and prompted bullying from some of his classmates.

On Monday morning, the college student made a video call to his father in distress.

"He said, 'Dad, I'm not feeling ok. I'm not thinking right … because of the bullies,' and I told him, 'Come home so that we can talk,'" Pierre Ronal Bel said in a statement.

Soon afterward, the Ohio State Highway Patrol says the 20-year-old got out of his Toyota Avalon on the shoulder of Interstate 70 and stepped into westbound lanes of traffic. The agency says its investigation remains open. Bel's family says they were told he took his own life.

"Police showed up at my door," his father said, "to report that my son had thrown himself under a truck."

Bel was among a growing number of Haitians in Ohio outfitted with the ankle monitors after the Trump administration ended Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, which allowed them to work legally in the US and protected hundreds of thousands of people across the US from deportation. Immigrant rights advocates are pointing to the young man's apparent suicide as they call for federal officials to stop using the monitors.

"Pierre died as a result of policy. And it's our immigration policy that took his life," Pastor Carl Ruby of the Central Christian Church in Springfield said at a news conference Tuesday, calling on Republican lawmakers to speak out and "put an end to the shackling program before other people end up taking their lives."

Immigration and Customs Enforcement says Bel applied for admission into the United States in Brownsville, Texas, in March 2024 and was released into the country by the Biden administration. The agency issued Bel an ankle monitor on July 29 while he continued his immigration proceedings.

Asked about reports that the student had died by suicide after facing bullying for wearing the device, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement spokesperson said in a written statement that the highway patrol's investigation into the death is ongoing.

"ICE does not comment on the cause of death while that investigation is pending, and we will not speculate about unverified claims regarding other individuals," the spokesperson said, reiterating the administration's push for undocumented immigrants to "self-deport."

"Remaining in the country illegally, while fighting removal, is a choice. Leaving with a free flight home and $2,600 is also a choice," the spokesperson said. "ICE will continue to use detention or alternatives to detention as needed (for) those illegal aliens who stay in violation of the law."

In a statement on its Facebook page, Wright State University did not directly address the bullying allegations, but said counseling and support services had been made available to students, faculty and staff.

"The safety and well-being of our students is the highest priority, and we remain dedicated to providing a campus community where every student feels safe, supported, included and welcomed," the statement said.

Wright State University President Sue Edwards said the school community was heartbroken.

"Pierre was an active honors student who was passionate about soccer and was already actively engaged in his classes and the campus community," she said. "The University mourns the death of Pierre and extends our deepest condolences to his family, friends and loved ones during this unimaginably difficult time."

According to his father, on Friday Bel said something had devastated him in his ROTC class at the school.

"He told me, 'Dad, I felt humiliated … Everyone got uniforms, except for me, because of the bracelet," Pierre Ronal Bel said.

Wright State said questions about the ROTC program and its participation requirements and uniform issuance should be directed to the United States Army Cadet Command.

A spokesperson for the US Army Cadet Command told CNN the ankle monitor wasn't the reason Bel did not receive a uniform. Bel was not eligible to become a cadet in the ROTC program because of his immigration status, the spokesperson said, and therefore was taking the class as an elective and could not be issued a uniform. Class leadership was "very supportive" of him joining the class, the spokesperson said.

In recent social media posts, Bel described the ankle monitor and how difficult it was for him to wear it.

"I came to this country to pursue my education. I didn't come here to commit a crime or hurt anyone. Yet now I'm walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience," he wrote in a July 30 Instagram post, which included a series of pictures of him at awards and recognition ceremonies.

"I came here to study, to build my future, and to live a better (life) not to be treated like criminal. So now, how am I supposed play college sports with a GPS monitor on my leg?"

The student also shared testimonials from Springfield High School teachers and coworkers at a Texas Roadhouse restaurant, apparently provided as letters of support in his pending immigration case, praising his work ethic and leadership skills.

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican who's been a vocal critic of the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for Haitians, told reporters Tuesday that Bel's death was a "horrible tragedy." And at a news conference Tuesday in Springfield, community leaders and immigrant rights advocates slammed the way they said authorities had treated Bel and other Haitians, many of whom have been living in fear since their deportation protections were revoked.

The ankle monitors are part of a frequently used ICE program known as "alternatives to detention." But advocates say that for many Haitians in Springfield, the devices evoke the painful history of shackles worn during slavery. The day before Bel's death, demonstrators marched in a protest dubbed "Unshackle Springfield."

Advocates estimate that ankle monitors have been issued to hundreds of Haitians in Springfield in the past month, and many in the Columbus area as well.

"There's nothing illegal or criminalizing about Pierre Damas Bel, not even a traffic ticket, and it shouldn't have to get to this point for this administration to understand that there's blood on their hands," said Yola Lamarre of the Haitian Community Network. "There's nothing just about shackling people that have not ever committed a crime. … This was a situation that could have been prevented."

Lamarre, who organizers described as a close friend and mentor to Bel, said she'd spoken with him multiple times about his concerns over the ankle monitor.

"Pierre shared a lot of depressive thoughts with me after we saw the ankle monitor situation being targeted to Haitians in Springfield," she said, tearing up as she described her friend to reporters. "Pierre Damas Bel was not a criminal, but he was treated as one."

CNN's Omar Jimenez and Lizzie Jury contributed to this report.

title: College coaches name Michigan football top sleeper team for 2026
description: College coaches are naming Michigan football as a top sleeper team this season under new coach Kyle Whittingham.
fullText:
There aren't many expecting Michigan football to make major waves this season, but there are some who think that the Wolverines may be better than a lot of people are expecting. And among them are college coaches.

With Kyle Whittingham taking over the program after a successful 21-year head coaching stint at Utah, there are hopes in Ann Arbor that his ability to get more out of less in Salt Lake City will translate to him getting more out of more at The Big House. And given that this might be the most talent he's ever worked with, it's an intriguing prospect that he could make a big impact right away.

The Athletic polled coaches anonymously across college football, and though there weren't the highest of expectations for the maize and blue, Michigan topped the entire landscape with three votes from coaches indicating that the Wolverines could be the biggest sleeper in the country.

One coach off the record oversees tight ends in the American Conference, and another was an offensive line coach from the Mountain West.

"I really want to see what Whittingham does at Michigan. They're so creative in the run game. I wouldn't be shocked if you blinked and they're 10-2." — American Conference tight ends coach

"I could see him with some of those Michigan guys with the Utah culture make them really good, really good fast. They have an identity, and it's the type of identity that they've wanted there." — Mountain West offensive line coach

Yes, the schedule is an absolute bear, but there's a reason why teams play the games -- because often preseason expectations don't equal regular season results. So while we can look at Oklahoma, Iowa, Penn State, Indiana, Oregon, and Ohio State on the schedule as a daunting slate, any of them could be worse than expectations, in concert with Michigan actually being better than expected. Last year, Penn State and Clemson were considered top-five teams in the preseason, and both finished unranked. LSU often starts in the top 10 and has struggled mightily since winning the national championship following the 2019 season.

But then there's the case of 2021 Michigan. The Wolverines were much better than anyone anticipated that year, having gone 11-1 that year, beating what was considered to be among the best Ohio State teams in recent history, 42-27, at The Big House. Could 2026 be a reprise of 2021? Given that this is a reset under Whittingham, and the team reportedly has solid player-led leadership, it could mirror that season perhaps -- though the road to Indianapolis and beyond is certainly much tougher than it appeared to be that year.
